title: Less to lose
hook: Diogenes' slave ran away, and Diogenes let him go; fewer things, fewer wounds (On Tranquility 8)

segments.voice: Yesterday: choose your company, because moods spread by contact. Your line was calm is catching. Who did you sit with, and what did you catch? Day four hundred ninety-nine.

Have you ever bought something nice and then spent a week worrying about it? The new phone you're scared to drop. The car you check from the window. The white sofa no one is allowed to eat on. It was meant to make life easier, and it came with a small, permanent alarm attached. In chapter eight of On Tranquility, Seneca says that of all the things that trouble the mind, the biggest is money and what it buys. And he tells a story about the philosopher Diogenes, the man who lived in a large clay jar, on the day his only servant ran away. Today: less to lose.
screen: `THE WHITE SOFA NO ONE CAN SIT ON.` → `A SMALL, PERMANENT ALARM.` → `DIOGENES' SERVANT RUNS AWAY.`

segments.voice: First, Seneca's claim. People with little, he says, often suffer less than people with much, not because poverty is pleasant, but because they have less that can be taken. It hurts less, he observes, never to have had something than to lose it. Fortune has fewer places to strike. Second, the story. Diogenes owned one slave, named Manes. Manes ran away. Someone told Diogenes where he'd gone, and Diogenes didn't think it worth the trouble to bring him back. His reason: it would be shameful if Manes could live without Diogenes, and Diogenes couldn't live without Manes. Third, the honest flinch. The story treats a human being as a possession, as Seneca's whole world did. Diogenes is talking about a man as if he were a lost coat, and readers today rightly feel that. But inside the story there's also something Diogenes may not have meant: Manes walked free, and Diogenes let him. Fourth, the point Seneca draws. He imagines Diogenes saying to Fortune: mind your own business, there's nothing of yours left here. Fewer things, fewer wounds. Seneca, who owned a great deal, isn't telling anyone to own nothing. He's asking which of your things own you. The phone you're afraid to drop. The status you'd hate to lose. Every one of them is a place where a bad day can reach in. Having less isn't the goal by itself. Being harder to wound is.
screen: `IT HURTS LESS NOT TO HAVE THAN TO LOSE.` · `MANES RAN; DIOGENES LET HIM GO.` · `THE HONEST FLINCH.` · `NOTHING OF FORTUNE'S LEFT HERE.` · then, large: `LESS TO LOSE.`

segments.voice: Look around you, or picture your home. Find one thing you own that you worry about more than you enjoy. Something that sets off a small alarm. Hold it in your mind. Imagine it gone: given away, sold, simply not there. Notice what happens in your chest. Relief? Panic? Both? If it's relief, you've found something you could let go. If it's panic, notice how much of you is tied to it. Either way, you've learned something. The bell holds the time.
Less to lose. Diogenes let his runaway servant go, and Seneca draws the lesson: fewer things, fewer places for Fortune to wound. Today's word.
Your line: less to lose. Let one possession go this week: give it, sell it, donate it. Start with the one that sets off the alarm. Day four hundred ninety-nine.

howItsDone: People practicing Stoic simplicity sometimes give away possessions that cause more worry than use, aiming to be harder to wound rather than simply to own less.

fork.setup: you're Diogenes. your only servant has run off, and someone tells you where he is. what do you do?
fork.reveal: Diogenes let him go: it'd be shameful if Manes could live without Diogenes, but not Diogenes without Manes.

original.note: Latin, 'Fortune, chance': which Seneca imagines Diogenes telling to mind its own business.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Stoics praised being poor.
what it means: Seneca praises being harder to wound; fewer things give Fortune fewer places to strike.
what a scholar hears: the Manes story also appears in Diogenes Laertius 6.55; it reflects a slave-owning world that both Seneca and Diogenes took for granted.

notes: On Tranquility 8 paraphrased: money as the greatest source of trouble; less pain in not having than in losing; Diogenes and Manes; 'Fortune, mind your own business; there's nothing of yours with Diogenes'. Confirm details and section.
